topic: Duct route and resistance: why short, straight runs work

slides.headline: Every bend costs you airflow.
slides.subline: The shortest run between hood and roof is the one that works.

slides.title: What slows the air
slides.intro: Resistance adds up before the fan ever sees it.

items.title: Bends
items.text: Two tight elbows can cost more than a longer straight run.

items.title: Length
items.text: Distance is fine, if the fan was chosen for that distance.

items.title: Narrow sections
items.text: One squeezed length strangles everything after it.

slides.note_text: A route on paper is cheaper to change than a route in steel.

slides.title: When the route is fixed
slides.intro: You can still choose the right fan for the building you have.

items.title: Measure the whole path
items.text: Not the straight line. The path the air actually travels.

items.title: Count every bend
items.text: Offsets, transitions and roof turns all take their share.

items.title: Match the fan to that
items.text: A fan sized to the hood alone will lose the fight.

slides.note_text: The outlet needs room to breathe, not a corner behind a parapet.

slides.headline: Send the route, we will check what it costs you.
slides.subline: A drawing and two photos are usually enough to start.

caption_en:
Most weak extractors are not weak fans. They are long, twisting ducts that nobody added up before the fan was chosen.

Air does not care about the straight line on the drawing. It follows the real path: up, across, around a column, through a narrow section, then out over the roof. Each of those turns takes pressure the fan has to pay for.

If the kitchen already exists, we measure the path as built and match the fan to it. If it is still on paper, we redraw the route while it is still cheap to change.
